claim: To land bombers in fog, wartime Britain set its runways on fire.

end.title: Operation Pluto
end.description: Undersea oil pipeline operation in World War II (1939–45)

knots.passage: The aviation travel industry is affected by the severity of fog conditions. Even though modern auto-landing computers can put an aircraft down without the aid of a pilot, personnel manning an airport control tower must be able to see if aircraft are sitting on the runway awaiting takeoff. Safe operations are difficult in thick fog, and civilian airports may forbid takeoffs and landings until conditions improve.
knots.hatnote: Fog still grounds planes, even with computers that can land them.

knots.passage: A solution for landing returning military aircraft developed in World War II was called Fog Investigation and Dispersal Operation (FIDO). It involved burning enormous amounts of fuel alongside runways to evaporate fog, allowing returning fighter and bomber pilots sufficient visual cues to safely land their aircraft. The high energy demands of this method discourage its use for routine operations.
knots.hatnote: In the Second World War, Britain tried a blunter fix: fire.

knots.passage: When FIDO was needed, the fuel pumps were started to pour flammable liquid into the pipe system and a Jeep with a flaming brand lashed to its rear drove fast down both sides of the runway to ignite the fuel at the outlets in the pipes. The burners were sometimes ignited by men on bicycles or by runners on foot. The result was a row of flame along the side of the runway that would warm the air. The heat from the flames evaporated suspended fog droplets so that there would be a clearing in the fog directly over the runway.
knots.hatnote: Lighting the runway was a hands-on job.

knots.passage: The device was developed by Arthur Hartley for British RAF bomber stations, allowing the landing of aircraft returning from raids over Germany in poor visibility by burning fuel in rows on either side of the runway.
knots.hatnote: It was developed by an engineer named Arthur Hartley.

knots.passage: Hartley also developed the pipes used in Operation Pluto (Pipe Lines Under The Ocean), a series of twenty-one undersea pipes used to transport oil from Britain to continental Europe to support the Liberation of Europe. The system supplied the allied armies with 1 million US gallons (3,800 m) of fuel per day during the advance into Germany, and Hartley received £9000 after the war for his work on Pluto from the Royal Commission on Awards to Inventors.
knots.hatnote: Burning fuel was one of his jobs; moving it was a bigger one.

knots.passage: One was established at Sandown on the Isle of Wight, and another at Dungeness on the Kent coast. Construction was carried out at night and in secret, and equipment was carried in under tarpaulins. The pumping stations and storage tanks were camouflaged to look like villas, seaside cottages, old forts, amusement parks and other innocuous features.
knots.hatnote: The pipelines needed pumping stations on the English coast, kept secret.

knots.passage: Although the pipeline itself is no longer in use, many of the buildings that were constructed or utilised to disguise it remain, especially on the Isle of Wight, where the former pumping station at Sandown is currently in use as a miniature golf facility.
knots.hatnote: Some of the disguises outlived the war.

payoff: The engineer who burned fuel to clear fog also piped it under the Channel, from pumps disguised so well one is now mini golf.
caveats: FIDO's invention is formally credited to J. D. Main-Smith; Arthur Hartley's page credits Hartley with developing it.
